title: Should Women Preach?
excerpt: Christians who hold the same Bible in the same esteem disagree about whether women may preach and pastor, and the texts, the history and the best case on each side all have to be heard.
body:
Few questions divide a church as quickly as this one, and few leave as many people hurt. In one congregation a woman who can plainly open the Scriptures and make them clear is told that the gift is real and that there is nowhere on Sunday for her to use it. In another, a family leaves after the church calls a woman as pastor, and they leave grieving, sure that the people they love have stopped listening to the Bible. A girl asks her father why the women at church never speak from the front, and he finds that he can't give the reason without hearing how it sounds. A husband and wife read the same chapter of 1 Timothy on the same evening and come away further apart.

Each side has a story about the other, and both are too easy. One story says that churches with women in the pulpit have simply given in to the culture. The other says that churches without them simply want to keep men in charge. Both things have been true of some churches. Neither comes close to explaining the serious people on the other side, most of whom got where they are by reading Paul.

## What the Bible Shows Women Doing

Begin with what nobody disputes, because there is more of it than either side tends to remember.

The Old Testament has its examples. "Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time" (Judges 4:4), and "the people of Israel came up to her for judgment" (4:5). The general Barak would not go to war without her. When King Josiah's officials needed to know what God was saying about the rediscovered book of the law, they went to "Huldah the prophetess" (2 Kings 22:14). Complementarians point out that Deborah was a judge and a prophet and not a priest, and that the book of Judges is hardly a picture of things as they should be. Egalitarians point out that the text introduces her without a word of apology.

Women were the first witnesses of the resurrection. Jesus sent Mary Magdalene to the apostles with the news, and she "went and announced to the disciples" what she had seen (John 20:18). Luke adds that when the women told the apostles, "these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them" (Luke 24:11). At Pentecost, Peter explained what was happening with a promise from the prophet Joel: "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy" (Acts 2:17). Philip the evangelist had four daughters "who prophesied" (Acts 21:9). In Corinth, Paul takes it for granted that a woman "prays or prophesies" when the church is gathered, and regulates only how she does it (1 Corinthians 11:5).

Then there is the last chapter of Romans, where Paul greets his coworkers by name and many of the names are women's. He begins with Phoebe, "a servant of the church at Cenchreae" and "a patron of many and of myself as well" (Romans 16:1–2). The word translated "servant" is the one translated "deacon" elsewhere, and since Paul commends her to the Romans at the head of the letter, most scholars think she carried it to them. He greets Prisca and Aquila, "my fellow workers in Christ Jesus" (16:3), naming the wife first. Acts says that when the gifted preacher Apollos came to Ephesus knowing only part of the story, "Priscilla and Aquila heard him" and "took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately" (Acts 18:26).

And he greets Junia. "Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me" (Romans 16:7). The Greek can also be read as saying that the two were outstanding among the apostles, and that is how the great preacher John Chrysostom read it in the fourth century. He had no doubt Junia was a woman, and he marveled at the devotion of a woman who "should be even counted worthy of the appellation of apostle."

Later readers were less sure what to do with her. When Chrysostom's sermons were printed in English in the nineteenth century, an editor added a note to that sentence. The note prefers a man's name, Junias, and says the name can't be Junia if Paul is calling the pair apostles, since "that a woman should have been an apostle is out of the question." Many English Bibles of the twentieth century printed Junias, a man's name that scholars have not found in any other ancient source. The text had been made to say what its readers already knew it had to say, and the church did that.

## The Two Passages That Say No

Against all of this stand two passages, and nobody who takes the Bible seriously can wave them off.

The first is 1 Corinthians 14. "The women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church" (1 Corinthians 14:34–35). Read alone, that is total. But the same letter, three chapters earlier, has women praying and prophesying aloud in the same gatherings. Whatever Paul forbids in chapter 14, it isn't every use of a woman's voice, and almost every interpreter on both sides agrees. Many who restrict the pulpit to men think Paul is barring women from the public judging of prophecies, which he has just described (14:29). Many who don't think he is stopping a particular disorder, wives interrupting with questions, which is why his remedy is to ask at home.

The second passage is the center of the whole debate. "Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet. For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor" (1 Timothy 2:11–14).

Three details matter here. The first is that Paul commands that women learn, which in his world was not assumed. The second is the phrase "exercise authority." It translates a Greek verb that appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and scholars still argue over whether it means simply to hold authority or to seize and misuse it. The King James translators chose "usurp authority." The third is the reason Paul gives. He doesn't appeal to custom in Ephesus or to what outsiders would think. He appeals to Genesis, to the order in which the man and the woman were made.

## The Complementarian Case

The name is recent, from the late 1980s, but the position is old. In its best form it runs like this.

Men and women are equal in worth, both made in God's image, both heirs of the same grace. They are also different, and the difference is part of the goodness of creation and not a result of the fall. In the family and in the church, God has asked men to carry a particular responsibility of leadership, and that is an order of service, a burden laid on them and not a prize. When Paul comes to the question of who teaches and governs the gathered church, he roots his answer in creation, before sin entered and before any culture existed. An instruction grounded there can't be set aside as a local arrangement for one troubled congregation. The qualifications for the overseer assume a man, "the husband of one wife" (1 Timothy 3:2). Jesus, who broke convention about women freely, taught them, traveled with them and appeared to them first, still chose twelve men as apostles.

To this the complementarian adds the weight of history. For nineteen centuries nearly every church in every place, Eastern and Western, read these passages the same way. It is possible that all of them were blind until our own generation. But a reading that appears only when the surrounding culture begins to demand it ought to make us suspicious of ourselves.

Complementarians do not all draw the line in the same place. Some hold that a woman may teach the gathered church under the authority of its elders and that only the office of elder is closed to her. Some ordain women as deacons, pointing to Phoebe. Others believe that preaching to the assembled church is the very thing Paul forbids. So the question in the title divides people who agree on nearly everything else.

## The Egalitarian Case

The egalitarian position is also older than its name, and its best form is as careful with the text.

It begins with the Spirit. The gifts are given "to each" as the Spirit wills (1 Corinthians 12:7, 11), and nothing in the lists of gifts sorts them by sex. Pentecost was announced as the day when daughters would prophesy alongside sons. Paul's coworkers included a woman deacon and patron, a woman who helped correct a preacher's theology, women who "labored side by side" with him in the gospel (Philippians 4:3), and, on the oldest reading, a woman counted among the apostles. If Paul had believed that creation itself forbids women to instruct men, his own practice would be hard to explain.

So the egalitarian reads 1 Timothy 2 as the letter presents itself. Timothy has been left in Ephesus to stop certain people from teaching false doctrine (1 Timothy 1:3). The second letter to Timothy describes false teachers finding their way into households and winning over women in particular (2 Timothy 3:6). Paul's answer has two parts: let these women learn, and until they have learned, they are not to teach or to dominate. The reference to Eve fits that situation exactly, since she is the Bible's first example of someone deceived. On this reading Paul is doing in Ephesus what he would do anywhere, stopping the untaught from teaching.

And the egalitarian reads Genesis differently. The man and woman are given rule over the earth together (Genesis 1:27–28). A husband's rule over his wife is first mentioned among the consequences of sin, in Genesis 3. If that is so, male rule is part of what Christ came to heal. Paul's own sentence points the direction: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). The church took a long time to work out what that meant for slaves, and in the end it did.

## What Each Side Fears

Complementarians fear a method, and the fear isn't foolish. If an instruction that Paul grounds in creation can be explained as a local measure, what can't be? They have watched churches that started here go on to treat other teachings of Scripture as products of their time, and they worry about what will be left for their grandchildren to believe. They also notice that Galatians 3:28 is about who inherits the promise, and that Paul wrote it without erasing every difference between Jew and Greek.

Egalitarians fear something just as serious. They see gifts that the Spirit gave being buried by the church that needs them. They see girls learning, without anyone saying it, that they are a lesser kind of Christian. And they have seen what a theology of male authority can become in the wrong hands, which is the part of this history we would rather skip.

## What the Church Has Done With These Texts

Around the year 200 the North African teacher Tertullian wrote to Christian women: "And do you not know that you are (each) an Eve?" He went on, "You are the devil's gateway." That is a long way from anything Paul says, and it was said by one of the most influential writers the Western church ever had. Contempt for women got into our tradition early and sat beside our reading of these passages for a very long time. A complementarian has to be able to say so without flinching, because the contempt has too often been presented as the doctrine.

Worse has been done. Women who told a pastor they were being beaten at home have been sent back with a verse about submission. Women who reported abuse by a church leader have been told to forgive, to stay quiet for the sake of the ministry, to consider what their accusation would do to a godly man. No passage in the Bible asks that of anyone. Abuse by a church leader should be reported to the authorities. If you need someone sooner, [Find Help](/help) lists hotlines for abuse and sexual assault.

No side of this debate is clean. Abusers have sheltered in churches with women in the pulpit as well as churches without, and a congregation's position on this question has never protected anyone by itself. But churches where men hold the authority have a particular duty here. Authority that can't be questioned is dangerous in anyone's hands, and Jesus said of the way rulers lord it over others, "It shall not be so among you" (Matthew 20:26).

The history has another side too. The church always had women it leaned on and then forgot. When a Roman governor investigated the Christians of his province around the year 112, the two Christians he chose to question under torture were enslaved women "who were called deaconesses." In 451 the Council of Chalcedon ruled on the age at which a woman could "receive the laying on of hands as a deaconess." Quaker women preached in the 1600s. In 1853 a Congregational church in New York ordained Antoinette Brown. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, churches that would not let a woman teach a mixed Sunday school class at home sent women across oceans to evangelize and to teach the Bible to anyone who would listen. The site's essay on [women in church history](/writing/women-in-church-history) tells more of this.

## How Much Rides on It

This is not a question the creeds settle. The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed confess who God is and what Christ has done, and they say nothing about who may preach. Churches that ordain women and churches that don't confess the same Trinity, the same incarnate and risen Lord, the same salvation by grace, and the same authority of Scripture. Each side is tempted to promote the question. Some complementarians treat it as a test of whether a person believes the Bible at all. Some egalitarians treat it as a test of whether a person believes in justice at all. Both moves turn a brother or sister into an enemy.

It is not a small question either. A church has to decide who will preach on Sunday, and it can't do both things at once. That is why Christians who honor each other still end up in different congregations over it. It belongs to the second order: weighty enough to shape a church, not weighty enough to define the faith. This essay sets the readings side by side and leaves the conclusion to the reader and the reader's church, because faithful Christians who love the same Bible have landed on both sides.

What can be said to everyone is harder than picking a side. If your church reserves the pulpit for men, the test of your position is the women in your congregation. Are they taught as seriously as the men? Are they heard? Are their gifts used everywhere your convictions allow, or only where it's convenient? Would a woman in trouble be believed? A church can hold the complementarian reading and still fail every one of those, and many have. If your church opens the pulpit to women, the test is whether you reached that practice by wrestling with Paul or by getting around him, and whether you can still be corrected by a text you don't like. A church can hold the egalitarian reading and fail that, and many have.

On Easter morning the risen Christ gave the first announcement of the gospel to a woman and sent her to tell the men. They thought it was an idle tale.

He had told her to go anyway.

*"And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy."* (Acts 2:17)

*"Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness."* (1 Timothy 2:11)

*"For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face."* (1 Corinthians 13:12)
